+# ADR 0001: Increase Pricing Cache TTL to 3600 Seconds
+
+## Context
+
+Our pricing service relies on caching to reduce load on the backend and improve response times for client requests. The cache is utilized by multiple downstream services that query pricing information frequently. Previously, the cache TTL was set to 900 seconds (15 minutes), which balanced freshness against cache efficiency. However, analysis of pricing update patterns revealed that actual pricing changes occur infrequently—typically no more than once or twice per day. The current 15-minute window creates unnecessary cache invalidations and backend queries, particularly during high-traffic periods when repeated freshness checks become costly.
+
+Additionally, our observation that the Anthropic prompt-cache TTL is 1 hour demonstrates that longer cache windows are operationally sustainable. The pricing data itself is relatively stable, with changes being deliberate and scheduled rather than continuous. These factors suggest that the existing TTL is overly conservative and creates performance drag without corresponding benefit to data freshness.
+
+## Decision
+
+We will increase the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This aligns the pricing cache behavior with our prompt-cache practices and accommodates the observed frequency of pricing updates. The change will be applied at the cache layer, affecting all services that consume the pricing cache without requiring downstream modifications.
+
+This decision assumes that a 1-hour maximum staleness is acceptable for pricing data and that the cost savings from reduced cache misses and backend queries justify the tradeoff. The change is reversible and can be adjusted based on operational metrics collected after deployment.
+
+## Consequences
+
+Reducing cache invalidation frequency will decrease backend load during peak traffic periods and improve response latency for pricing queries. Services will see fewer unnecessary cache misses, reducing the computational overhead of cache validation and backend requests. The 1-hour window provides a comfortable margin for handling pricing updates while still capturing changes within a reasonable timeframe.
+
+However, clients will experience up to a 1-hour delay in seeing newly published pricing changes. For use cases requiring real-time pricing precision, this represents a notable change from the previous 15-minute guarantee. We must clearly communicate this window to clients and establish monitoring to detect pricing staleness issues. If this proves problematic in practice, we can implement a cache invalidation mechanism triggered by pricing update events to regain immediate consistency when needed.
